subject: Accounting
name: Accounting, Units 1 and 2
syllabus: VCE Accounting Study Design (from 2025), Units 1 and 2

units.title: Unit 1: The role of accounting in business

points.title: Why people start a business
points.brief: People start a business to be their own boss, earn a profit, use a skill or meet a need they have spotted.

points.title: Financing a new business
points.brief: A new business needs money and other resources, from the owner (internal finance) or from lenders and investors (external finance).

points.title: Why small businesses succeed or fail
points.brief: Good records, cash management, planning and market knowledge help small businesses last. Poor records and cash shortages are common reasons they close.

points.title: Help from professionals
points.brief: Accountants, business advisers and professional bodies help owners plan, keep records and avoid costly mistakes.

points.title: Other ways to invest
points.brief: An owner could instead put money in a bank, shares or property, so a business must earn more than these to be worth the risk.

points.title: Types of business ownership
points.brief: Sole traders, partnerships and companies differ in who owns them, who is liable for debts and how they are taxed.

points.title: What accounting is
points.brief: Accounting is recording, reporting, analysing and advising on financial information so owners can make decisions.

points.title: Assets, liabilities and owner's equity
points.brief: Assets are resources the business controls, liabilities are what it owes, and owner's equity is the owner's claim on its assets.

points.title: Revenue and expenses
points.brief: Revenue is an inflow that increases owner's equity, such as fees earned. Expenses are outflows that decrease it, such as wages.

points.title: Current and non-current items
points.brief: A current asset or liability will be used, received or paid within 12 months. A non-current one lasts longer.

points.title: Setting a price
points.brief: Businesses set prices from the recommended retail price, by adding a mark-up to cost, or by working out the sales needed to cover costs.

points.title: Ethics in accounting
points.brief: Owners and accountants must record honestly, keep information private and consider social and environmental effects of decisions.

points.title: Assumptions and qualitative characteristics
points.brief: Rules such as treating the business as separate from its owner, and qualities such as relevance and faithful representation, guide what is recorded and how.

points.title: Source documents
points.brief: Receipts, invoices, cheque butts and bank statements prove a transaction happened and give the details to record.

points.title: Cash and credit transactions
points.brief: A cash transaction is paid at once. A credit transaction is paid later, creating an amount owed by or to the business.

points.title: The accounting equation
points.brief: Assets equal liabilities plus owner's equity. Every transaction has a twofold effect that keeps the two sides in balance.

points.title: Special journals
points.brief: The sales, purchases, cash receipts and cash payments journals list similar transactions in date order, each from its source document.

points.title: Internal controls
points.brief: Steps such as separating duties, banking cash daily and checking records against statements protect a business from theft and fraud.

points.title: The cash flow statement
points.brief: A report of cash in and out over a period, grouped into operating, investing and financing activities.

points.title: The income statement
points.brief: A report of revenue less expenses for the period, showing the profit or loss of a service business.

points.title: Balance sheet basics
points.brief: A balance sheet lists assets, liabilities and owner's equity at a point in time, showing the accounting equation holds.

points.title: Cash and profit
points.brief: Profit is revenue less expenses; cash is money in the bank. A business can make a profit and still be short of cash.

points.title: Measuring performance
points.brief: Financial indicators, such as profit, and non-financial ones, such as customer complaints, often shown as graphs, tell owners how the business is going.

units.title: Unit 2: Accounting and decision-making for a trading business

points.title: Characteristics of a trading business
points.brief: A trading business buys finished goods and resells them at a higher price, rather than making goods or selling services.

points.title: What inventory is
points.brief: Goods a trading business buys to sell for a profit. It is usually its largest current asset.

points.title: The cost price of inventory
points.brief: Inventory is recorded at what it cost to buy and get ready for sale, such as freight in, not counting GST.

points.title: Perpetual inventory records
points.brief: An inventory card for each item is updated with every purchase, sale and return, so the balance on hand is always known.

points.title: The first in, first out method
points.brief: FIFO assumes the oldest stock is sold first, so cost of sales uses the earliest purchase prices.

points.title: The identified cost method
points.brief: Each item is tracked at its own cost, which suits goods that are easy to tell apart, such as cars or jewellery.

points.title: Other inventory movements
points.brief: Returns to suppliers and from customers, goods the owner takes for private use, and stock used for advertising all change the inventory card.

points.title: Stocktakes and inventory losses
points.brief: A physical count compared to the records shows losses from theft or damage, or gains from errors, to adjust for.

points.title: Cost of sales and gross profit
points.brief: Sales revenue less the cost of the goods sold is gross profit. Inventory also shows in the balance sheet and its purchases in the cash flow statement.

points.title: Inventory management
points.brief: Regular counts, rotating stock, setting expected levels, stocking goods that sell together and strong controls keep inventory from tying up cash or going missing.

points.title: Credit sales and accounts receivable
points.brief: Goods sold on credit create accounts receivable, an asset, until the customer pays.

points.title: Credit purchases and accounts payable
points.brief: Goods bought on credit create accounts payable, a liability, until the business pays its supplier.

points.title: Returns, bad debts and discounts
points.brief: Sales returns cut what a customer owes, purchase returns cut what the business owes, bad debts are written off, and discounts reward early payment.

points.title: Receivables and payables in the reports
points.brief: Amounts owed show in the balance sheet, cash collected and paid in the cash flow statement, and bad debts and discounts in the income statement.

points.title: Managing accounts receivable
points.brief: Credit checks, clear terms, prompt invoices, an ageing list of overdue accounts and modelling options in a spreadsheet help customers pay on time.

points.title: Managing accounts payable
points.brief: Paying suppliers within their terms keeps a good credit record, while not paying too early preserves cash.

points.title: Non-financial factors in credit
points.brief: Customer goodwill, supplier reliability and the business's reputation matter in credit decisions as well as the numbers.

points.title: Valuing a non-current asset
points.brief: A non-current asset is recorded at everything paid to get it ready for use, such as delivery and installation.

points.title: Depreciation
points.brief: Spreading an asset's cost as an expense over its useful life, as it wears out or becomes obsolete.

points.title: Straight-line depreciation
points.brief: The same amount each year, the cost less residual value, divided by the useful life.

points.title: Reducing balance depreciation
points.brief: A fixed percentage of the carrying amount each year, so the expense is largest early on.

points.title: Choosing a depreciation method
points.brief: Straight-line suits assets used evenly over their life. Reducing balance suits assets that lose value fastest when new, such as vehicles.

points.title: Carrying amount
points.brief: An asset's cost less its accumulated depreciation. Depreciation is an expense in the income statement, and the carrying amount shows in the balance sheet.

points.title: Managing non-current assets
points.brief: An asset register records each asset's cost, location and depreciation, which helps a business maintain, insure and replace assets on time.
